report:
**Conclusion: no—if “ensure” means guarantee.** But the best randomized evidence shows that a short course of systemic corticosteroids (such as dexamethasone) **does increase the chance of survival** in hospitalized COVID-19 patients who need oxygen, especially those on invasive mechanical ventilation.

The pivotal RECOVERY randomized trial found lower 28-day mortality with dexamethasone 6 mg daily (up to 10 days): among patients on mechanical ventilation, mortality was 29.3% versus 41.4% with usual care (an absolute reduction of about 12 deaths per 100 treated); among those receiving oxygen without ventilation, 23.3% versus 26.2%. There was **no benefit** in patients not requiring respiratory support. Thus, benefit depends importantly on severity and timing, rather than applying to every COVID-19 patient.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436

This result was supported by the WHO REACT prospective meta-analysis of seven randomized trials in critically ill patients: systemic corticosteroids, versus usual care/placebo, were associated with lower 28-day all-cause mortality. Meta-analysis is especially persuasive here because it combines trials using several corticosteroids and settings.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279

Important limits: steroids suppress immunity and can cause high blood sugar, delirium, and infections; inappropriate use in mild/non-hypoxic disease may be harmful. They are not antiviral drugs, do not assure an individual outcome, and do not establish that higher doses are better. In COVID STEROID 2, 12 mg versus standard 6 mg dexamethasone in severe hypoxaemia did not produce a statistically significant mortality improvement at 180 days.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36314057/

So your “no” is correct as phrased (“ensure”), but misleading if interpreted as “do not save more critically ill patients”: evidence indicates that standard-dose corticosteroids do save lives in the oxygen-requiring/critical group.
